author: Ethan Goode
title: NAACP targets universities in the south amidst voting rights controversy - NewsBreak
text:
By Ethan Goode ,
2 hours ago
BATON ROUGE, La. (Louisiana First) — A growing national debate involving voting rights, college athletics, and political representation is now placing Louisiana — and LSU — at the center of a broader civil rights conversation.
The NAACP and members of the Congressional Black Caucus are calling on colleges and athletic conferences across the South to take stronger positions on what they describe as attacks on Black voting power.
The push comes amid ongoing legal and political battles tied to congressional redistricting in Louisiana, including discussions surrounding districts represented by Cleo Fields.
Civil rights leaders argue that schools and athletic programs that benefit from Black athletes and Black communities should not remain silent on issues impacting representation and voting rights.
“The issue is whether institutions that benefit from black talent, black labor and black communities are willing to speak out when black political power is under attack,” said Congresswoman Yvette D. Clark (D-NY).
LSU has not publicly commented on the matter as of Wednesday, but Baton Rouge has increasingly become part of the national discussion due to the university’s visibility within the SEC and college athletics.
Advocates behind the movement say the effort is about more than sports.
“This is bigger than sports, this is about democracy,” said Congressman Troy Carter.
The debate is unfolding as lawmakers and athletic leaders across the country continue discussions surrounding NIL reform and the future of college athletics governance.
Supporters of federal NIL legislation argue changes are needed to stabilize what many describe as an increasingly chaotic system for student-athletes.
“This is going to support student athletes and the educational mission of college athletics. Really important critical stuff to get the NIL kind of madness under control,” said Speaker of the House Mike Johnson (R-La.).
But some activists say they are prepared to intensify pressure on major athletic conferences, including the SEC, until schools and political leaders take stronger stances on voting rights concerns.
“If the SEC schools are for it, we are against it,” said Congressman Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY).
The controversy now leaves Louisiana at the intersection of sports, politics, race, and representation — with Baton Rouge becoming part of a rapidly growing national conversation.
